mqud.title: The dataset
intro: Download the JSONL for a flat table of questions, figures, and paper passages. The Hub viewer groups the same information into nested fields.
facts: `question`, `answer`, `question_type`, and `difficulty`. Each answer is extracted from the paper.
`image` gives the image path. `paper_title`, `paper_abstract`, and `figure_caption` supply the context.
`source_text` and `source_paragraphs` contain the supporting passages. Use `paper_id` to group questions from the same paper.
All 1,250 examples are in the Hub’s `train` split; the release has no separate test split.

code.label: Read one question
code.text:
import json
from urllib.request import urlopen

revision = "295b4efc36226ad19429edcd4bccc151b72971d0"
url = (
    "https://huggingface.co/datasets/lingchensanwen/mqud/"
    f"resolve/{revision}/data/mqud.jsonl"
)
with urlopen(url) as response:
    row = json.loads(response.readline())

print(row["id"], row["paper_id"])
print(row["question"])
print(row["answer"])
print(row["image"])
code.after: The `image` value is a path in the dataset repository.

qsalience.title: Try QSalience
intro: Start with the example files in the repository, or supply your own questions and article.
facts: A CSV with two columns: `question` and `sentence_id`.
A text file with sentences numbered from 1. Only the text through `sentence_id` is passed to the model.
`T5_predictions.csv` contains one predicted salience score per question, in input order. The scale runs from 1 to 5.

code.label: Run with T5
code.before: In a local checkout, install the README dependencies, then run:
code.text:
cd code/preprocess
python preprocess.py \
  --question_csv_path example_question.csv \
  --article_txt_path example_article.txt

cd ..
python predict_salience.py \
  --model_name t5 \
  --input_file preprocess/example.json
code.after: Preprocessing writes `example.json`. The second command loads the released T5 model and writes the predictions.

qudsim.title: Scores and document pairs
intro: Read the published scores below, or use the demo notebook to compare your own texts.
facts: `dataset/similarity.json` has 650 rows. Each row includes document IDs, segment scores, and a `Similarity` value.
The notebook accepts JSON or CSV with `Document 1`, `Document 2`, `Model 1`, and `Model 2` columns.
Level 0 keeps questions specific to the content; level 1 abstracts it. New comparisons require the repository’s API setup.

code.label: Read the scores
code.text:
import pandas as pd

revision = "f146127b870e866c661ab67a04da5122f9b6805a"
url = (
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AlliteraryAlligator/QUDsim/"
    f"{revision}/dataset/similarity.json"
)
scores = pd.read_json(url)
print(scores[["Source ID", "Target ID", "Similarity"]].head())

notes: In the linked CLI version, `--unique` and `args.with_replacement` refer to different names. Use `demo.ipynb` until this is corrected.

qudeval.title: Human annotations
intro: The CSV contains 2,190 questions and their human judgments. The source articles are linked separately in the data README.
facts: `questions` contains the text; `system` records where it came from.
`essay_id`, `anchor_id`, and `answer_id` locate the article and the two sentences needed to evaluate the question.
`criteria1` through `criteria4` contain the annotations. Label definitions are in the paper.

code.label: Read the CSV
code.text:
import pandas as pd

revision = "62eeb3df2ee3e382c878eb0eb92fecd2c1fe6d04"
url = (
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lingchensanwen/QUDeval/"
    f"{revision}/data/data-collection.csv"
)
annotations = pd.read_csv(url, index_col=0)
columns = ["essay_id", "anchor_id", "answer_id", "questions", "system"]
print(annotations[columns].head())

notes: Some judgments were revised after submission to resolve annotator disagreement. The example uses a fixed data revision so the results can be checked.

elabqud.title: Question–target annotations
intro: There are 2,878 question–target annotations for 1,299 elaborations. An elaboration may have more than one annotation.
facts: `file_num` identifies the article; `elab_line` gives the line containing the added explanation.
`question` is the implicit question. `target` and `target_line` locate the earlier text that prompted it; `worker_num` identifies the annotator.
Full Newsela articles require separate access. The data README links the source-text access route.

code.label: Read the TSV
code.text:
import pandas as pd

revision = "8a253a8f014c642d5156333313f9d1573a031767"
url = (
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sheffwb/elabQUD/"
    f"{revision}/data/targets_and_questions.tsv"
)
annotations = pd.read_csv(url, sep="\t")
print(len(annotations))  # 2878 question–target pairs
print(annotations.groupby(["file_num", "elab_line"]).ngroups)  # 1299

qud-parsing.title: Run the parser
intro: The Colab notebook runs the pipeline from numbered sentences to questions and their anchors.
facts: Put one sentence per line in `inputa/`, with a sentence number, a tab, and the sentence.
For each answer sentence, predict an earlier sentence that raises the question.
Generate candidate questions from the predicted anchor, then rank them.
Each question labels an edge between the answer sentence and its anchor.
notes: The original setup uses the bundled Transformers code and separate model downloads. Follow the repository’s environment instructions.

contextweaver.title: How context is built
intro: After each step, ContextWeaver updates the dependency graph and prepares the context for the next action.
facts: Represent the latest history entry as a node in the graph.
Rank earlier steps by dependency likelihood and keep up to `m` parents. Exclude nodes marked Failed or Superseded.
After warmup, collect the selected parents and their ancestors, up to the `W`-node limit.
Keep the selected entries in full and compress the others. Preserve their original order.
notes: During warmup, the agent receives the full history. Algorithm 1 gives the complete procedure.

bilingual-disfluencies.title: What the models predict
intro: We fit one logistic regression classifier per disfluency type for each speaker group. GPT-2 provides word surprisal; the classifiers also use lexical, syntactic, and phonetic features.
facts: Broken words and repetitions of sounds or syllables.
notes: Training and test sets are separated by participant. Features of the preceding and following words are analyzed separately.
